analysis.one_liner: Doubles federal tobacco taxes and adds a new tax on vaping nicotine.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have roughly doubled the federal cigarette tax and taxed vaping nicotine for the first time, never got a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would roughly double the federal excise tax on cigarettes (from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand) and roll-your-own tobacco, and sharply raise taxes on pipe tobacco, smokeless tobacco, and cigars so all tobacco products are taxed at similar rates. It would also create a brand-new federal tax on the nicotine used in vaping products, while exempting nicotine used in FDA-approved quit-smoking drugs like gum and patches. Tax rates would rise with inflation each year, and sellers would owe a one-time tax on inventory on hand when the increase took effect.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gains would have gone to public health and the federal Treasury. Higher prices are the best-documented tool for cutting smoking, especially among teenagers, and the bill was designed to close a loophole: cheaper products like pipe tobacco and vaping were taxed far less than cigarettes, giving companies a way to sell nicotine cheaply. Nicotine replacement products approved by the FDA would have been spared the new tax, keeping quitting aids relatively cheaper.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the federal cigarette tax from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand and doubles the roll-your-own tobacco rate from $24.78 to $49.56 per pound [S3].

Raises taxes on the cheaper alternatives to near cigarette levels — pipe tobacco jumps from about 2.8 cents to $49.56 per pound, small cigars from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand — so companies can no longer undercut the cigarette tax by switching product type [S3].
Creates a first-ever federal excise tax on nicotine extracted, concentrated, or synthesized for vaping, taxed at the cigarette-equivalent rate per 1,810 milligrams [S3].
Exempts nicotine used in FDA-approved or investigational drugs (such as nicotine gum, patches, and lozenges sold as medicine), so FDA-approved quitting aids stay untaxed [S3].
Indexes all the tobacco tax rates to inflation starting after 2023, so their value no longer erodes each year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers and vapers, through higher prices — excise taxes are almost entirely passed through to the retail price. Because smoking is now concentrated among lower-income households, the burden would fall hardest on working-class smokers. Tobacco and vaping manufacturers, importers, and retailers would also pay: higher taxes on their products, a one-time tax on inventory they held when the increase took effect, and new permit and bonding requirements for anyone making or importing nicotine.

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: lower-income smokers spend a larger share of their income on cigarettes, so doubling the tax takes a bigger bite out of a low-income household's budget than a wealthy one's — the health benefit comes through a tax on the people, not on industry profits [S3].

The bill imposes a one-time 'floor stocks' tax on anyone holding tobacco inventory when the rates rise, with only a $500 credit per person — a real cash burden for small distributors and retailers caught with stock on hand [S3].

Revenue and health gains both depend on people keeping buying: if high prices push smokers to untaxed black-market or cross-border products instead of quitting, the bill raises costs on compliant sellers without delivering the health benefit.
The large-cigar tax switches from a percentage of price to a flat per-pound rate, which changes who pays how much in ways that would need Treasury guidance to sort out [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits this is a genuine trade-off, not a giveaway. Doubling tobacco taxes and taxing vaping would very likely reduce smoking and youth vaping, which saves lives and medical costs over time — but the instrument is a consumer tax, so the upfront cost lands on smokers, who today are disproportionately lower-income working people. The bill's design strengths are real: closing the cheap-product loopholes and exempting FDA-approved quitting aids push people toward quitting rather than just charging them more. An honest supporter would acknowledge that a heavy excise tax is a blunt and regressive way to get there.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL) introduced the Tobacco Tax Equity Act of 2023 on September 26, 2023 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over taxes, on the day of introduction [S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind: no subcommittee or full committee action, no report, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a single House Democrat, and never had a bipartisan base of support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, tobacco and vaping companies and sellers kept the current, lower tax structure, and smokers' prices stayed unchanged. No one gained the public-health or revenue benefits the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco and vaping sellers kept status quo

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would double tobacco excise taxes and create a new vaping nicotine tax.

for.name: 1 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after it was referred to his committee; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee took no action after the referral, so the bill never came near a vote.

industries.industry: Tobacco manufacturers (cigarettes, cigars, smokeless, pipe and roll-your-own)
industries.note: The bill would roughly double excise taxes on their products and equalize rates so cheaper product lines could no longer dodge the cigarette tax. Their interest in keeping rates low runs against the public-health goal of making tobacco more expensive.

industries.industry: Vaping and e-cigarette industry (nicotine extractors, concentrate makers, vape manufacturers)
industries.note: A brand-new federal tax on extracted, concentrated, or synthesized nicotine would raise their costs and retail prices for the first time, and they would face new permit and bonding requirements as tobacco-product manufacturers.

industries.industry: Tobacco and vape retailers and distributors
industries.note: Higher taxes shrink sales, and a one-time floor stocks tax with only a $500 credit hits inventory on hand when rates rise. Small shops bear this alongside the industry, but the same higher prices serve the health goal.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical makers of FDA-approved nicotine replacement therapy
industries.note: Nicotine used in FDA-approved drugs (gum, patches, lozenges sold as medicine) is explicitly exempt from the new tax, making approved quitting aids relatively cheaper than vaping products. Their product competes for the same nicotine users, on the side of quitting.
